edition.notes: The title page identifies the William Peter Feeney 2014 Memorial Edition. The preceding imprint leaf prints ISBN 978-1-62292-058-7, '2014 Printing by: Loreto Publications,' and says this edition derives from a copy of the original 1859 Haydock supplied to Catholic Treasures by the Slaves of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. A following leaf identifies that source as the Dunigan and Brothers 1859 unabridged edition. This record describes the exact modern printing digitized as Internet Archive item haydock-douay-rheims-catholic-bible; it does not re-identify that scan as an 1859 artifact.

C. 1060' on artifact p. 396; the close of that chapter immediately before 1 Kings 21 remains marked A.M. 2944 on p. 398; and the next chapter begins in A.M. 2944 on p. 399. Between those bounding year marks, 1 Kings 21:10-15 narrates David's flight to Achis, king of Geth, his fear, and his feigned madness.
passages.notes: Read directly in artifact PDF pages 396, 398, and 399, visible printed pp. 366, 368, and 369. The A.C. 1060 line stands at 1 Kings 20, not beside the Achis verse itself; the passage therefore records the edition's continuous chronological frame rather than pretending the verse carries an independent date. The commentary on 21:10 is compiled under the edition's ordinary initials and names Salien, Haydock (H.), Sanchez, Menochius (M.), and Calmet (C.); none of them is treated as the author of the uninitialled year markers.

passages.context: The superscription prints Psalm 30 as Davidic. In the note to verse 1, Haydock's compiler voice (H.) transmits several traditional settings: flight from court, with Calmet (C.) cited to 1 Kings 19 and 27; imminent danger in the desert of Maon, with 1 Kings 23:25, Kimchi, and Du Pin cited; Absalom's conspiracy, attributed to Theodoret and Menochius (M.); an episode associated with Eusebius; and the captives, associated with Chrysostom. The page supplies no numerical date for the Psalm.
passages.notes: Read directly in artifact PDF page 742, visible printed p. 706. This record preserves the initials and named authorities instead of attributing every alternative to Haydock personally. The Maon chronology must be supplied, if used, from the separate 1 Kings 23 passage rather than invented from this Psalm note.

passages.context: The printed superscription of Psalm 70 names David, the sons of Jonadab, and the former captives. Its verse-1 note explains the Septuagint addition through the Rechabites and those first carried into captivity, ending that statement with Challoner's initial (Ch.). A following chronology explicitly attributed to Usher gives the first captivity under Joakim as A.M. 3398, the second under Jechonias as A.M. 3405, and the last, when Jerusalem was destroyed and Sedecias was taken, as A.M. 3416. The same note later says that this captivity material is absent from the Hebrew and from several copies of the Septuagint and calls the title of no great authority, with Calmet (C.) and Berthier (Bert.) among the printed attributions. It separately preserves interpretations in the voice of the captives, of David persecuted by his son, and, more sublimely, of Jesus Christ.
passages.notes: Read directly in artifact PDF page 776, visible printed p. 740. The A.M. figures belong to an Usher-attributed chronological paragraph in the commentary on Psalm 70:1; they are not printed in Psalm 88, do not prove the Babylonian proposal preserved in the Psalm 88 note, and are not attributed personally to Haydock. This record makes no B.C. conversion and does not use the qualified Greek title as a textual control for the Hebrew superscription.

passages.context: The superscription prints Psalm 88 'for Ethan, the Ezrahite.' The note to verse 1 preserves competing historical attributions instead of resolving them: a proposal marked to Calmet (C.) places its composition with a captive at Babylon lamenting the destruction of Juda's kingdom under Sedecias; a proposal ending with Worthington's initial (W.), with an intervention marked H. after 'person,' allows David to have written in the person of Ethan or Idithun. The note then says that most of the Fathers explain the Psalm of Christ's kingdom. Verse 51 asks the Lord to remember the reproach of his servants, borne in the Psalmist's bosom, 'of many nations.' The verse note marked H. explains the nations as continually insulting the servants and blaspheming God's name; Calmet (C.) associates the burden in the bosom with poignant grief and discusses alternative textual renderings involving many peoples.
passages.notes: Read directly in artifact PDF page 793, visible printed p. 757, for the superscription and verse-1 note, and artifact page 795, visible printed p. 759, for verse 51 and its note. The record does not decide among direct Ethan authorship, Davidic composition in another's person, or the Babylonian-captive setting; it records the alternatives and their printed initials. It supplies no numerical date, does not identify the reproaching nations with one specific historical enemy, and does not treat an individual commentator's proposal as the Psalm's inspired superscription.

passages.context: The superscription prints 'A prayer of Moses, the man of God.' The accompanying note calls this the Jewish legislator's characteristic title, cites Berthier (Bert.) and Du Hamel (D.), then preserves real attributional diversity: Menochius (M.) proposes David composing in Moses' name; Jerome is cited for Moses' authorship extending to the following untitled Psalms through Calmet (C.); Tirinus (T.) and Augustine are brought into the discussion; Calmet also allows a descendant of Moses during the captivity or a Davidic prediction. The page itself assigns no numerical wilderness date.
passages.notes: Read directly in artifact PDF page 795, visible printed p. 759. The record positively preserves the Mosaic superscription while distinguishing it from the commentary's competing authorship proposals. It cannot by itself verify a date such as 1491-1451 B.C.; a publication using that range needs a separate chronology witness.

work.author: George Leo Haydock, compiler
work.description: Haydock's annotated Douay-Rheims, first issued in parts from 1811 and reprinted through the nineteenth century. The commentary is a compilation of Catholic exegetes with initialled attributions: C. for Calmet, H. for Haydock, M. for Menochius, W. for Worthington, and others, expanded in the edition's own key. The scriptural text it prints is Challoner's revision; the notes are the work registered here. A locus is BookToken.chapter.verse.
work.title: The Douay-Rheims Bible with a Comprehensive Catholic Commentary
